content.thinking:
I'm designing a koala figure gripping a eucalyptus branch stand, with a wooden base plinth and a vertical trunk post forming a fork for the koala to cling to.

Settling on a design: a horizontal branch supported by posts for the koala's butt and feet, with a second branch in front at chest height for the arms to grip, like a Y-shaped stand. I'm working out scale — a sitting koala roughly 0.6-0.7m tall — and planning the coordinates for the plinth and branch heights accordingly.

I'm refining the upper branch curve with interpolated hand positions at z=0.17, then positioning the koala's seated body on the lower branch—butt resting near y=0.33, torso rising as a pear-shaped ovoid toward the chest around y=0.62.

Now I'm sketching the overall koala proportions: hips at 0.34, chest at 0.50, neck at 0.60, head center at 0.68, with ears topping out near 0.80, giving a total sitting height close to real koala scale. I'm starting to lay out the skeleton hierarchy, beginning with a root hip joint and spine chain.

I'm defining the spine as a catmull chain of four points running from hips up to the neck base, and then building a separate neck chain branching off it toward the head joint, parenting each appropriately.

For the head itself, I'm setting it to parent off the neck's tip joint with a slight forward-facing direction, assigning it the "head" role, then adding a jaw joint positioned just below the head's origin.

I'm placing the head's center using relative offsets like forward and up rather than raw axis coordinates, since that avoids confusion about which direction is which — using the same word-based local coordinate system I saw in the decal example for consistency.

Setting the head sphere's radius to about 0.125 with a slightly stretched scale (1.1 wide, 0.95 tall and deep) to roughly match koala head proportions relative to the body width, confirming scale applies in world axes since there's no orientation option on the part function.

Now I'm placing the facial features: a small jaw box beneath, a protruding black oval nose scaled wider than tall near the top-front of the face, and a lighter cream muzzle sphere just below it, all positioned using offsets from the head's world center.

For the eyes I'm considering a small pixel-art texture on a plane rather than a plain box, positioning tiny beady koala eyes just beyond the head ellipsoid's surface facing forward.

Now I'm placing the fluffy details—white chest fur, chin ruff, and the big round ears positioned at the sides of the head, angled outward with scaled sphere geometry, bringing the total head height to about 0.865.

Still working out ear geometry...

For fringe tufts I'm scattering cards across the ear surface filtered by rim normals, keeping the API usage conservative since I can't test it directly. For the body I'm considering a loft along the spine chain, using the hips-to-spine bone path to drive the skin shape.

Now I'm sketching the koala's pear-shaped torso stations, defining width and depth at each height from the butt upward, with section rx mapping to sideways width and ry to front-back depth along the path's normal.

I need to watch the rounded end caps -- the lowest section's cap can extend further down than expected, which risks clipping into the branch the koala sits on. I'm adjusting the bottom point's height so the body rests just above the branch's top surface instead of overlapping it.

Laying out the spine chain from hips through spine joints to neck, then placing the head joint and sphere center so it overlaps the neck and torso properly, adjusting the head's position and radius to get the bottom edge to sit right.

Now I'm raising the ears and head geometry to fit the overall height (~0.88 total), acknowledging the koala looks a bit larger than real scale but deciding it's fine as a stylized proportion. Next I'm working on fur shading, planning a countershaded belly using a cell-paint function with a texel size and a ramp of gray tones.

Writing fur shading code...

Now I'm working out the arm geometry, positioning shoulders, elbows, and hands so the forelimbs reach forward and down to grip the branch, while keeping the flat color palette minimal within the pixel kit's limits.

I realize the branch position is too close, putting it right against the chest, so I'm shifting the branch further forward and up to give the arms room to wrap naturally, recalculating shoulder-to-hand distances to confirm they fit within the limb lengths.

Now I'm setting up the limb chain for each arm with shoulder, elbow, and hand joints, naming them per side (L/R based on positive/negative X), and defining tapered tube radii along the arm for the fur-covered limb mesh.

For the hands, I'm designing a koala-style grip with fingers curling around the branch: each hand gets a few finger chains (accounting for the koala's two opposable digits) as short 2-joint arcs wrapping over the branch, keeping total joint count within the 160 limit across all four limbs.

Working out finger placement angles around the branch's circular cross-section, picking points that wrap from the back-top over the front so the hand looks like it's gripping the branch naturally.

Still working out finger positions and claw placement...

I need to fix the parenting for the finger chain, attaching it to the correct arm joint tip, and reconsider the upper branch geometry to make it a straighter path rather than the curved one I initially sketched.

Working out the branch curve coordinates...

Now I'm thinking through leg placement for the koala sitting posture, with hips, knees, and feet positioned to straddle and grip the lower branch.

Checking the leg segment lengths against the foot target near the branch, the knee bend comes out way too sharp given the short hip-to-foot distance — I need to reposition the foot further out to get a more natural fold.

Let me reposition the lower branch to z=0.02 so the butt rests back-top while feet grip the front edge, placing foot targets around (±0.17, 0.31, 0.04). Calculating hip-to-foot distance gives about 0.115, so the knee should lift forward-out and upward to bridge that reach.

Now I'm working out the toe placement, wrapping each foot's toes over the branch's front curve using the branch radius plus toe offset, and adjusting the ankle angle so the foot sits toward the top-back of the branch rather than slipping behind it.

Checking the knee bend for the hind leg given the short hip-to-foot distance, I test thigh/shin lengths of 0.13/0.12 versus 0.11/0.10 and compute the interior knee angle via the law of cosines -- settling on roughly 53°, a deep but plausible squat-like fold, which fits the outward knee position better than the sharper 45° option.

I'm working out the `limb` function's bend parameter typing -- deciding to just pass a plain direction vector rather than a nested array, since the signature accepts root/target/lengths/bends/opts and returns a Vector3 array that can feed directly into `chain` as a three-point path, with the hips joint serving as the root parent for the hind limb.

Positioning the hip, spine, and shoulder joints to connect the arm chain to the chest, then thinking through tube skinning for the arms and simple four-toed hind feet. I'm skipping a tail since koalas don't have one, maybe adding a small fluffy rump bump instead, and setting up hinge-role ear joints on the head that angle outward and up.

For the fur, I'm designing a pixel-art tuft texture using a greyscale grid pattern tinted by each part's color, sketching a small triangular tuft shape in a 5x7 grid.

Still writing fur patterns...

Then I'm deciding where to scatter these tufts — along ear rims, cheeks, chin ruff, and chest — using small card sizes with a lean angle, scattering around 40 hits across the head surface filtered to only the upward-facing normals.

Ears keep the default outward flow. For the torso, I'm scattering cream tufts on the chest filtered by normal and height, flowing downward, and using the body sweep surface as the scatter target with a seeded rng for placement.

For the branches, I'm painting eucalyptus bark with cellPaint — blending pale cream, grey-green, and tan patches using stretched noise to create vertical streaks that mimic peeling bark along the branch length.

I'm building a reusable bark-paint factory that stretches the noise axis differently for trunk (vertical) versus branches (along their own curve), picking from a bark color ramp. Next I want to add the eucalyptus leaves themselves — slender blue-green lance-shaped leaf cards hanging from the branch tips.

Designing leaf pixel art...

Good, leaf tip at bottom works. Now I need to place leaves along the upper and trunk branches using some kind of path-sampling helper that generates frames along a sweep, oriented with their outward normal facing away from the branch surface.

Actually, manually sampling points along the branch with varying parameter and small random angle offsets is safer than relying on an ambiguous callback-based helper -- I'll loop through t-values, get each frame via the branch's point-at-angle method, and attach leaves there leaning outward and bending downward with a flow direction that flattens them against the surface.

Since upward-facing frames have a horizontal plane, I'm varying the flow vector per leaf using cosine/sine of the index so they fan out in different horizontal directions, with a decent lean and bend for a hanging leafy look, sized small, roughly a dozen or so per branch across a spread of angles. I'm also planning to cap the trunk top with a cluster of upward-facing leaf frames for extra fullness there.

Thinking about rigging now: frames placed by raw coordinates bind to the nearest joint automatically, which is risky since something like the trunk cap could accidentally snap to the koala's hip or spine joint and move when the koala animates. The fix is to introduce a dedicated static "root" joint at the base of the stand, separate from the koala's "hips" joint, so the stand geometry binds to root and stays put while hips (parented to root) drives the character's movement.

Now I'm designing the plinth and trunk: a tapered catmull-rom trunk sweep rising from the base with shrinking radius and rounded caps, and a plinth built from a tiled wooden box with planked texture, trim, moss patches, pebbles, grass tufts, leaf litter cards, and small gumnut details on the branch.

I'm checking overall proportions -- the 1.0 x 0.6 base needs to contain the koala's extended limbs and the trunk/branch positions, with the plinth top sitting at y=0.07 and the trunk base sunk slightly into it. I'm also verifying the lower branch height clears the plinth with enough room for the koala's feet, and considering adding a support post beneath the branch for structural believability.

Now I'm working out the fur and surface colors -- using the pixel-paint texel approach for the torso and head, dark grey for ears with white insides, a flat black nose with a small highlight box, and cream-colored claws against darker grey fur on the hands and feet to keep the flat-color palette manageable.

For the limbs and chest I'm applying the same positional cell-paint logic to keep continuity, restricting the cream chest patch by normal direction and position, and darkening the paws separately. For the eyes I'm building a tiny pixel-art texture (black pupil, white sclera) scaled up and mapped onto a small plane for each eye.

Now I'm working out the facial geometry in detail: the dark mouth line sits between muzzle and jaw, and I'm sizing and positioning the protruding muzzle sphere, checking that it extends slightly beyond the head's front surface for a natural koala snout shape.

I'm adjusting the nose placement so it sits high on the muzzle and comparing its height against the head top and eye positions, aiming for proportions where eyes sit just above nose level.

Now I'm checking the overall head dimensions—working out the ear placement relative to the head's top radius, and realizing the total height comes out too tall, so I'm lowering the ears slightly to bring the proportions back in line with a real koala's size.

Working out eye and ear placement relative to the scaled head sphere...

Now I'm positioning the muzzle and nose spheres so they protrude correctly from the head's front face, checking that the nose top aligns near the eye line.

Still positioning head features, now working out the jaw box, mouth line, and ear placements with inner ear surfaces for depth.

I'll keep the inner ellipsoid rotation matching the outer ear's. Now setting up the ear joints parented to the head, and defining the head joint position with the neck chain feeding into it as the parent.

For the spine, I'm using 4 points to create 3 named spine segments, with the final one aimed toward the neck point, and the parent joint is the previous spine joint. I'll loft the torso through these station centers with catmull interpolation, matching radii at each point, and add a pot-belly bulge for that koala silhouette.

For attachments, I'm placing shoulder spheres where the arms meet the torso, haunch spheres at the hips to blend the thighs, and considering a small tail nub versus a cream-colored rump patch, which real koalas have, applying a paint rule based on the surface normal's z-value to mark that area.

I'm also planning ear tufts using scattered cards on the ear geometry filtered by upward-facing normals, adding chest cream patches, small gumnut spheres along the branches, and a wood-plank textured plinth with a palette-based draw function.

Working out the texel density for the plinth so planks tile cleanly across the top and sides, then considering adding a thin moss-green layer on top for a grassy finish.

I'm restructuring the plinth as a wood base topped with a moss mat, setting the floor level where tree roots join, then planning fallen leaf cards scattered on the moss using leaf-textured sprites.

Now I'm adding grass tuft cards to the moss layer, sketching out a small pixel texture pattern for green spiky grass blades.

I'm also deciding to paint the moss surface with a dithered green noise instead of a flat tile texture, while keeping the plinth sides as textured wood tiles. Then I'm sketching small decorative props -- grey pebble boxes and tiny lathe-based mushrooms with red caps near the trunk base.

Mapping out the mushroom cap using a sphere hemisphere geometry with small white box dots for spots, checking part counts stay reasonable, and planning to add eucalyptus leaves along the trunk top and branch ends. I'm also listing out which helper imports I'll need -- paint utilities, texture kit functions, and path helpers -- before defining the color palette, starting with a snapped fur ramp.

Still defining color ramps...

Now I'm writing the fur paint function, using noise and cell position to determine chest region boundaries while being careful not to overlap with the head's paint zones.

Still writing fur shader logic...

Setting up fur paint for the torso, then writing a generic limb-building function with a bark-pattern helper. Now working through the arm placement, positioning shoulder and hand targets symmetrically on each side with inward-curving limb geometry.

Building the arm chains with elbow hints, then sweeping tapered radii along each arm for a natural limb shape, capping with a palm sphere at the hand joint.

Now I'm working out finger placement, computing offset positions and curling angles for each finger around the hand using trig to space them evenly.

Setting up the finger chains with naming conventions and radius profiles so each digit tapers properly, then adding a claw spike extending from the last joint point.

Now working out the hind leg toe placement: computing the ankle target position on the lower branch circle, then setting the hip joint location and spreading the toe angles roughly from -35 up through 125 degrees for a natural splayed foot.

I'm setting up the hind limb chain with hip, knee, and ankle joints with appropriate lengths, checking that the total reach covers the distance to the foot target, and now I'm checking whether the folded knee angle causes the thigh and shin tubes to visually overlap.

I'm verifying positions relative to the torso—confirming the hip sits outside the torso's half-width at its height, the knee angles outward enough to clear the body, and that the lower branch geometry doesn't clip through the torso or feet placement.

Checking the branch's tapering radius and toe clearance, the numbers are close enough to be visually acceptable. Now I'm defining the upper branch's curve path with its own set of control points and radii.

I'll add a midpoint to keep that segment straight, and apply the same fix to the lower branch, then start sketching a small end twig sweeping upward from the branch tip.

Now I'm setting up the leaf card placement along the branch using sampled frames at varying positions, configuring each card's size, lean, bend, flow direction, and random variation to scatter the leaves naturally.

I'm defining two eucalyptus leaf color palettes—a darker green-blue set and a lighter one—so the leaf textures alternate variants for visual variety, randomly assigned via the rng.

For the trunk top and branches, I'm placing gumnut spheres at underside frame positions along branch sweeps using small brown-tinted geometry attached with a bone reference, then adding fur tuft textures tinted a pale greenish-white at surface hit points for the head covering.

Now I'm scattering cheek ruff cards on the head surface filtered by normal direction and height range, giving them a lean and flow angle with a light grayish tint, plus similar scattered tufts on the ears and chest with their own size, density, and color filters based on normal and position.

For the environment I'm adding floor litter and grass cards using the frame utility for orientation, scattering grass around the base corners with cross-shaped leaning cards, and finishing the plinth with dark wood corner trims and a small front plaque idea, possibly with a simple eucalyptus leaf icon since rendering text in pixels is tricky.

Designing plaque pixel texture...

Confirming the leaf stamp placement fits within bounds, with plane size set small. For the mushroom, I'll keep it simple with a stem cylinder and a hemisphere cap sphere, adding a couple near the top-right corner with some dot details.

I'm also placing a few rotated pebble boxes in varied grays, making sure each part attaches to the correct bone -- root for stand pieces, head for facial features, jaw for mouth parts -- so the rig weights align properly.

Writing blob helper function...

Still sorting out imports...

Finishing the imports and pruning unused ones like polyline, then setting up metadata and constants for the texel size and degree-to-radian conversion.

Now I'm writing the fur color painting logic, defining a noise-based cell shader that randomly assigns fur shades with occasional darker or lighter outliers, and carving out a cream-colored chest patch based on position and surface normal.

Continuing the head paint function, blending cream cheeks with fur shading based on noise and surface normal. The cheek region sits in the lower third of the head sphere, and I'm applying the same logic to the muzzle area for a consistent cream patch. Now moving on to painting the ears.

Writing bark texture code...

Still writing wood tile texture...

Now I'm adding a moss-covered box for the floor top, setting GROUND at y=0.081 to align with the floor surface, then planning dark corner cap boxes for the plinth feet.

I'm positioning a front-facing plaque plane and checking overall model proportions—trunk and leaf cluster pushing the total height toward roughly 0.95-1.05, which feels acceptable against the koala's 0.8 scale. Now I'm sketching the curved trunk path coordinates that bend upward and outward as it rises.

I'm fixing the branch attachment points so they align precisely with the trunk's x-position at each height, then adding a few small spike "knobs" along the trunk for texture detail. I'm also placing a support post rod with rounded bark texture and flat caps to brace the structure, before moving on to work on the eyes and remaining facial features.

Now I'm scattering leaf litter cards across the ground using randomized positions and rotations, with mirrored flow directions for natural variety, then starting on a batch of grass frames placed near the mossy edges of the scene.

Working through the joint hierarchy next -- defining the jaw as a child of the head, then setting up the head and neck joints with their positions, directions, and roles, building out the chain structure one span at a time.

Still placing ear joints and parts...

The inner ear pokes out about 1.6cm, which looks good. For the ear cards I'm scattering white card hits across the ear parts, with bones placed by hit location at the ear joint. For eyes I'm using plane parts attached to the eyes bone, skipping brows but adding a highlight, and now I'm setting up the nose blob with its dark color and position.

Adding nose highlight and muzzle shape...

I'll simplify by skipping the separate mouth line and instead adding a dark lip box at the jaw front to create the visible mouth line, then move on to foot pad blobs for the ankle area before continuing with the shoulder.

Adding shoulder and haunch fur blobs anchored to the spine and hip joints, skipping a separate rump blob since the torso loft already covers that region, and double-checking the belly front position relative to the torso stations before building out the torso loft with bone spine stations...

Finishing the torso loft sizing and cap checks, then setting up the hip joint with its parent/direction and verifying the single-root-joint requirement is satisfied before attaching the hind limb to the hips joint.

Now I'm double-checking type correctness across the file—making sure position arrays, limb bend parameters, and chain path inputs all match expected Vector3/array signatures, and confirming the chain options like parent and role literals infer correctly when passed as inline object literals.

Writing sweep frame logic...

I need to avoid cluttering leaves near the hands on the upper branch, so I'll skip leaf placement around the middle of that branch where x is near zero, instead positioning leaves only toward the branch ends—roughly t=0.08–0.14 on one side and t=0.8–0.98 on the other.
